```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_torch <- torch::torch_is_installed()
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
```

A molecule is a graph: atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Molecular
property prediction is graph classification or regression with node
features (the element, charge, aromaticity) and edge features (the bond
order). This article shows how to build such graphs, how to split them by
scaffold so that test molecules are structurally new, and how to train an
edge aware GIN.

graphlearnR does not parse SMILES strings or compute chemical scaffolds.
Use a chemistry toolkit such as RDKit (in Python, or through an R
interface) to get atoms, bonds and Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and pass them
to graphlearnR as plain vectors and tables.

## Atoms and bonds

`molecule_graph()` takes element symbols and a bond table. Atoms become a
one hot encoding over a list of common elements plus an "other" column;
bonds become a one hot encoding of the bond order (1, 2, 3, and 1.5 for
aromatic) on both directions of each bond.

```{r}
# acetic acid, heavy atoms only: C-C(=O)-O
acetic <- molecule_graph(
  atoms = c("C", "C", "O", "O"),
  bonds = data.frame(from = c(1, 2, 2), to = c(2, 3, 4), order = c(1, 2, 1))
)
acetic
acetic$x[, c("C", "O", "other")]
cbind(t(acetic$edge_index), acetic$edge_attr)
```

Element and bond order vocabularies can be changed with `elements` and
`bond_orders`. Further atom features (formal charge, hydrogen count) can be
added by binding columns to `g$x` before training.

## A synthetic data set

`dataset_synthetic_molecules()` generates small random molecules with a
carbon backbone that is either a chain or a ring of five or six atoms,
with random nitrogen and oxygen atoms and side chains. The label says
whether the molecule has a ring. The molecules are synthetic and carry no
chemical meaning; they exist to demonstrate the workflow without
downloading anything.

```{r}
mols <- dataset_synthetic_molecules(200, seed = 1)
labels <- vapply(mols, function(m) as.character(m$graph_y), "")
table(labels)
scaffolds <- attr(mols, "scaffold")
head(sort(table(scaffolds), decreasing = TRUE))
```

## Scaffold splits

A random split puts near copies of the same scaffold in training and test,
which overstates how well a model generalizes to new chemistry. The
scaffold split of MoleculeNet (Wu et al. 2018) groups molecules by
scaffold, sorts the groups from largest to smallest, and fills training,
then validation, then test. No scaffold appears in two parts.

```{r}
sp <- split_graphs(length(mols), method = "scaffold", groups = scaffolds)
lengths(sp)
intersect(scaffolds[sp$train], scaffolds[sp$test])
table(labels[sp$test])
```

Because the largest group (here every acyclic molecule) goes to training,
the test set of a scaffold split can have a very different label mix from
training. Report the label distribution of each part along with the
metrics.

## Training an edge aware GIN

`gnn_model("gin", edge_dim = ...)` uses GINE layers, which add the bond
features to each message, and sum pooling gives one vector per molecule.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model <- gnn_model("gin", input_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$x), hidden_dim = 32,
                   output_dim = 2, num_layers = 3, pool = "sum",
                   edge_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit <- train_graph_model(model, mols[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                         val_data = mols[sp$val], epochs = 40, batch_size = 32,
                         seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, mols[sp$test])
```

For comparison, a random stratified split:

```{r, eval = has_torch}
sp_r <- split_graphs(length(mols), labels = labels, seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model_r <- gnn_model("gin", ncol(mols[[1]]$x), 32, 2, num_layers = 3, pool = "sum",
                     edge_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit_r <- train_graph_model(model_r, mols[sp_r$train], "graph_classification",
                           val_data = mols[sp_r$val], epochs = 40, batch_size = 32,
                           seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_r, mols[sp_r$test])
```

## Real data: MUTAG

MUTAG (Debnath et al. 1991) holds 188 nitroaromatic compounds labeled by
mutagenicity on bacteria, distributed with the TU graph kernel benchmarks
(Morris et al. 2020). graphlearnR does not ship it; `download_tu_dataset()`
fetches the archive from the TU Dortmund site, checks its checksum, and
reads it. Node labels (the element) become one hot node features and edge
labels (the bond type) become edge features. The chunk below is not run
when this article is built, so building the documentation never downloads
data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mutag <- download_tu_dataset("MUTAG")
mutag
graphs <- lapply(seq_along(mutag), function(i) mutag[[i]])
y <- vapply(graphs, function(g) as.character(g$graph_y), "")
sp <- split_graphs(length(graphs), labels = y, seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model <- gnn_model("gin", ncol(graphs[[1]]$x), 64, 2, num_layers = 4, pool = "sum",
                   edge_dim = ncol(graphs[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit <- train_graph_model(model, graphs[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                         val_data = graphs[sp$val], epochs = 100, batch_size = 32,
                         early_stopping = 20, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, graphs[sp$test])
```

MUTAG is small, so test metrics vary a lot between splits. Repeat over
several seeds or use cross validation and report the spread, not one
number; see the evaluation article. MUTAG does not come with SMILES, so a
scaffold split needs the structures from another source.

## Open Graph Benchmark data

The Open Graph Benchmark (Hu et al. 2020) distributes molecular data sets
such as ogbg-molhiv with fixed scaffold splits. `download_ogb()` fetches
and unpacks a data set, checked against a recorded checksum where one is
known (each OGB data set has its own license; check it before use),
and `read_ogb_graph()` reads its CSV files into a list of graphs with the
official split in its metadata. The package ships a two graph toy copy of
that layout, used here so that building this article downloads nothing.

```{r}
toy <- read_ogb_graph(system.file("extdata", "ogbg-toy", package = "graphlearnR"))
length(toy)
toy$metadata$split
toy[[1]]
```

For the real data:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hiv <- download_ogb("ogbg-molhiv")   # downloads, extracts and reads
lengths(hiv$metadata$split)   # 32901 4113 4113
```

OGB atom and bond features are integer codes; embed them or one hot encode
them before training. `read_ogb_node()` reads node property data sets such
as ogbn-arxiv in the same way.
